title: Priests, Forbidden Practices, and a Prophet Like Moses
summary: Moses sets out the support of the Levitical priests, who own no land because the LORD is their inheritance. He forbids every form of divination, sorcery, child sacrifice, and consulting the dead, and promises instead that God will raise up a prophet like Moses. The chapter ends with a test for telling a true prophet from a false one.
story:
Moses is still describing the offices that will lead Israel in the land. The section that begins at 16:18 deals with judges and officials, then the central court (17:8-13), the king (17:14-20), the priests (18:1-8), and the prophet (18:9-22). S. Dean McBride (Polity of the Covenant People, 1987) called this part of Deuteronomy Israel's constitution, because it divides authority among offices and places every one of them, even the king, under the written law. Chapter 18 completes the pattern.

The chapter answers a practical question every people in the ancient world faced: how do we know what the divine will is? Canaan's answer was divination and magic, reading omens and consulting the dead. Israel's answer is the word of God given through a prophet. The need was pressing, because Moses is about to die (his death comes in chapter 34), and the people who once begged him to stand between them and God's voice (5:23-27) need to know that God will keep speaking. The promise of a prophet like Moses echoed through the rest of the Bible. By the time of Jesus it had become a hope for one particular prophet still to come, and the New Testament names Jesus as that prophet.
historical:
The setting is again the plains of Moab before the crossing of the Jordan. The priestly arrangements assume the situation Deuteronomy describes elsewhere: the tribe of Levi received no territory but forty-eight towns scattered through the other tribes (Numbers 35:1-8; Joshua 21), and Deuteronomy's law of one central sanctuary (chapter 12) would leave country Levites without their old local altars. Verses 6 to 8 protect such a Levite. When Josiah centralized worship in Jerusalem around 622 BC, 2 Kings 23:9 records that the priests of the high places did not serve at the Jerusalem altar, though they ate unleavened bread among their brothers; scholars since Julius Wellhausen have discussed whether this shows the law going unenforced or the exclusion of priests who had served at illegitimate shrines (compare Ezekiel 44:10-14).

The practices listed in verses 10 and 11 were real, learned, and widespread. In Mesopotamia the barû, a trained diviner, examined the liver of a sacrificed sheep, and scribes compiled vast omen series: Bārûtu for livers, Enūma Anu Enlil for signs in the sky, Šumma ālu for events on earth. Clay models of sheep's livers, used to train diviners, have been excavated at Mari on the Euphrates (eighteenth century BC) and at Hazor in northern Israel. Ezekiel 21:21 pictures the king of Babylon shaking arrows, consulting household idols, and looking at a liver to choose his road. Prophets were known outside Israel too: letters from Mari record ecstatic prophets delivering messages from gods to the king, and a plaster inscription found in 1967 at Deir Alla in Jordan, from about 800 BC, tells of a night vision of Balaam son of Beor, the seer of Numbers 22 to 24. The contrast in this chapter is therefore not between having prophets and not having them, but between a God who speaks on his own initiative and techniques for extracting knowledge from the gods and the dead.

Child sacrifice heads the list. Deuteronomy 12:31 speaks of the nations burning their sons and daughters, and the Judean kings Ahaz and Manasseh are said to have made their sons pass through the fire (2 Kings 16:3; 21:6), a practice associated with the Topheth in the Hinnom Valley outside Jerusalem (Jeremiah 7:31; 2 Kings 23:10). In the Phoenician colony of Carthage, a sacred precinct held thousands of urns with the cremated remains of infants and animals, deposited over several centuries; Lawrence Stager and Samuel Wolff (Biblical Archaeology Review, 1984) read it as evidence of child sacrifice, a reading still debated among physical anthropologists. Otto Eissfeldt (1935) argued that molk in Punic inscriptions was a term for a kind of sacrifice, a view many scholars apply to the biblical Molek. Whether the biblical phrase always meant killing the child or sometimes a dedication rite is debated; Moshe Weinfeld argued for the latter (1972), while George Heider (The Cult of Molek, 1985) and John Day (Molech, 1989) argued for actual sacrifice.

Israel's own history shows how attractive these practices remained. Saul, who had banned mediums, consulted one at Endor the night before his last battle (1 Samuel 28). Isaiah mocked those who consulted the dead on behalf of the living (Isaiah 8:19), and Josiah removed mediums and spiritists as part of his reform (2 Kings 23:24). The hope for a prophet like Moses stayed alive long after. Deuteronomy's last chapter says that no prophet had since arisen like Moses (34:10). 1 Maccabees 4:46 and 14:41 postpone decisions until a trustworthy prophet should arise. The Qumran Community Rule looks for the coming of a prophet and the messiahs of Aaron and Israel (1QS 9:11), and the Testimonia (4Q175), copied in the early first century BC, quotes verses 18 and 19 as the first of its texts about the figures of the end.
cultural:
The Levites had no tribal territory, so they depended on the worship of Israel for their food. Their portion of an ordinary sacrifice was the shoulder (literally the foreleg), the two cheeks, and the stomach, together with the firstfruits of grain, new wine, and oil and the first fleece of the flock. Leviticus 7:31-34 assigns the priest a different portion, the breast and right thigh of a peace offering, and the rabbis reconciled the two by applying Deuteronomy's list to animals slaughtered for food away from the altar (m. Chullin 10:1). Critical scholars more often see two traditions of priestly dues. Either way, the Levites' support came from a whole people's giving, and their lack of land became a sign: the LORD himself was their inheritance (verse 2; Numbers 18:20). The Psalms later make that the prayer of any believer, “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup” (Psalm 16:5; compare 73:26). Paul applies the same principle to the support of gospel ministers (1 Corinthians 9:13-14), and Jerome, writing to the young priest Nepotian in AD 394 (Letter 52), connected the word clergy (from the Greek kleros, lot or portion) with this idea: the cleric's portion is the Lord.

The forbidden practices in verses 10 and 11 are a deliberate catalogue of the religious technology of the ancient world. Some are ways of reading the future from signs: divination by lots, arrows, or livers (qesem), soothsaying (perhaps from clouds), and interpreting omens, the verb used of Joseph's silver cup (Genesis 44:5). Some are ways of controlling events by ritual power: sorcery and casting spells, probably by tying magical knots. Some seek knowledge from the dead through a medium (ov) or a spiritist (yiddeoni, a knowing one). Rites for feeding and consulting dead ancestors are attested at Ugarit and in Mesopotamia, and 1 Samuel 28 shows what an Israelite expected a medium to do. The list is headed by child sacrifice, the most extreme form of the same instinct: to secure the future by paying unseen powers whatever price they demand.

What unites the list is the assumption that the unseen world can be read or managed by technique. Israel's God refuses to be managed. He speaks when he chooses and through whom he chooses, and his people are to listen. The word translated blameless in verse 13 (tamim) is used of a sacrificial animal without defect and of Noah and Abraham (Genesis 6:9; 17:1); here it means undivided, not hedging one's bets with other powers. The death penalty for a false prophet (verse 20) reflects the same seriousness: to speak in God's name what he has not said, or to speak for other gods, was to counterfeit the channel God had given. Later Jewish law handed such cases to a court (m. Sanhedrin 11:1, 5), and Jeremiah 26 shows a trial in which the elders cite the earlier prophet Micah to acquit Jeremiah.
literary:
The chapter has two halves joined by a contrast. Verses 1 to 8 are regulations about priestly support, framed by the statement that the LORD is Levi's inheritance (verses 1 and 2). Verses 9 to 22 are a sermon built on an opposition between the nations, who listen (yishmau) to diviners, and Israel, who must listen (tishmaun) to the prophet God raises up (verses 14 and 15). The same verb frames the choice.

The central promise is given twice. In verse 15 Moses speaks: God will raise up a prophet like me. In verse 18 Moses quotes what God said at Horeb: I will raise up a prophet like you. Between the two stands the memory of the assembly at Horeb (verses 16 and 17), when the people asked not to hear God's voice again and God approved their request (compare 5:23-28). The prophet is thus presented as God's answer to Israel's own plea for a mediator. The chapter plays on the verb darash, to seek: Israel must not seek the dead (verse 11), and God will seek an account from anyone who will not hear his prophet (verse 19).

The section closes with a question the reader might ask in his heart (verse 21) and its answer (verse 22), a teaching device Deuteronomy uses often (compare 7:17; 8:17; 9:4). The test of verse 22 is paired with Deuteronomy 13:1-5, which warns that even a prophet whose sign comes true must be rejected if he leads Israel after other gods. Read together, the two passages give a negative test by results and a positive test by loyalty. Within the larger section on offices (16:18 to 18:22), the prophet comes last, and he alone is raised up directly by God rather than appointed, chosen by lot, or inherited.

outline.t: The LORD is the Levites' inheritance
Equal shares for a Levite who comes to the sanctuary
No divination, sorcery, or consulting the dead

doctrines.note: Deuteronomy 18:18 is the Old Testament's definition of a prophet: one in whose mouth God puts his words, who speaks all that God commands. Prophecy is God's provision for his people's continuing guidance after Moses, measured by faithfulness to that word, and the chapter gives Israel a way to recognize presumptuous speech.

God makes himself known by speaking, not by being discovered through omens or manipulated through ritual. The contrast between the nations' techniques and Israel's prophet is the contrast between reading signs and hearing a word, and God approves a human mediator as a mercy to people who could not bear his voice.

Christian theology names prophet as one of Christ's three offices, with priest and king. Eusebius (Church History 1.3) already linked the anointed prophets, priests, and kings of Israel with Christ, and Calvin (Institutes 2.15) developed the threefold office. Peter identifies Jesus as the prophet of this chapter (Acts 3:22-23).

Divination, magic, consulting the dead, and child sacrifice are all ways of trying to secure the future from powers other than the LORD. The chapter calls them detestable and treats idolatry as something learned by imitating neighbors (verse 9), and it offers a better way: trusting a God who speaks.

Whether first read as one prophet or a succession, the promise pointed beyond itself once 34:10 said none had equaled Moses. By the first century it had become part of Israel's hope for the figures of the end (1QS 9:11; 4Q175), and the New Testament identifies Jesus as the prophet to whom Israel must listen (Acts 3:22-23; John 6:14).

words.note: Navi, prophet. The noun occurs more than 300 times. Its origin is debated; many connect it with an Akkadian verb meaning to call, so that a navi is one called or one who calls out. Its usage is clearer than its etymology: Exodus 7:1 calls Aaron Moses' navi, his spokesman, and verse 18 defines a prophet as one in whose mouth God puts his words. A prophet is measured by faithfulness to the message, not by foretelling as such, though foretelling is part of the message.

Nachalah, inheritance. It occurs about 220 times and usually means a family's allotted land, held in trust and passed down through generations (Numbers 27; 1 Kings 21:3). The Levites receive none, and verses 1 and 2 say that the LORD himself is their inheritance, a claim the Psalms take up in personal prayer (Psalm 16:5-6). Israel as a whole is also called the LORD's nachalah (Deuteronomy 32:9), so the word runs both ways.

To'evah, abomination, detestable thing. It occurs about 117 times and names what is abhorrent, whether to God or to people (Genesis 43:32 uses it of Egyptian scruples). Deuteronomy uses it about 17 times for idolatry (7:25-26), unclean food (14:3), and dishonest weights (25:16). Here it appears three times in verses 9 and 12, for the practices and for the person who does them: the verdict falls on a whole way of approaching the unseen.

Qasam, to practice divination. The verb occurs about twenty times and the related noun qesem about eleven. It covers attempts to discover hidden knowledge through lots, arrows, or omens (Ezekiel 21:21), and it is the first of the divinatory practices in verse 10, right after child sacrifice. Balaam is called a qosem (Joshua 13:22), and the later prophets use the verb for the false seers who told Israel what it wanted to hear (Micah 3:6-7; Ezekiel 13:6).

Ov, medium, the spirit of the dead or the pit through which it was summoned. It occurs about sixteen times, usually paired with yiddeoni, spiritist (Leviticus 19:31; 1 Samuel 28:3; Isaiah 8:19). Harry Hoffner (1967) connected it with a Hittite word for a ritual pit used to call up spirits from the underworld. The Septuagint rendered it engastrimythos, one who speaks from the belly, reflecting the belief that the voice seemed to come from below.

Tamim, whole, complete, blameless. It occurs about 90 times, many of them of sacrificial animals without defect (Leviticus 1:3), and also of people of integrity such as Noah and the one Abraham is called to be (Genesis 6:9; 17:1). In verse 13, tamim tihyeh im YHWH, it means undivided in trust. The Septuagint rendered it teleios, the word Jesus uses in Matthew 5:48 for being perfect as the heavenly Father is perfect.

Darash, to seek, inquire, require. It occurs about 165 times and is the ordinary verb for inquiring of God through a prophet (1 Kings 22:8) and for seeking God in worship (Deuteronomy 4:29). The chapter uses it twice: the forbidden practitioner seeks the dead (verse 11), and God himself will require an account of anyone who ignores his prophet (verse 19). Israel is to seek the living God; the God who is not sought by technique will seek out those who refuse his word.

Qum, to rise, and in the causative stem to raise up or establish. The verb occurs more than 600 times. In verses 15 and 18 God will raise up (yaqim, aqim) a prophet, the same verb used of God raising up judges (Judges 2:16), a king's offspring (2 Samuel 7:12), and a faithful priest (1 Samuel 2:35). It stresses that the prophet is God's appointment, not a self-appointed voice, and Peter plays on it in Acts 3:22-26, where God raises up his servant.

christ:
This is one of the clearest Old Testament promises that the New Testament applies to Jesus, and the expectation it created is visible before the New Testament was written. When Deuteronomy's last chapter noted that no prophet had arisen like Moses, whom the LORD knew face to face (34:10), it left the promise open. Qumran's Testimonia placed verses 18 and 19 first in a chain of end-time texts, and the Samaritans, who inserted verses 18 to 22 into their text of Exodus 20, came to expect the Taheb, a restorer like Moses; the Samaritan woman's expectation of a Messiah who will explain everything (John 4:25) fits that hope. In John's Gospel people ask John the Baptist whether he is the Prophet (John 1:21), and after the feeding of the five thousand, a Moses-like sign of bread in the wilderness, the crowd says, “Truly this is the Prophet who is to come into the world” (John 6:14).

Peter, preaching in the temple after Pentecost, quotes verses 15 and 19 and identifies Jesus as the prophet like Moses whom the people must hear (Acts 3:22-23), and Stephen cites the promise in his defense (Acts 7:37). At the transfiguration, when Moses himself appears with Jesus, the voice from the cloud says, “Listen to Him!” (Matthew 17:5), echoing the command of verse 15. Wayne Meeks (The Prophet-King, 1967) traced how John's Gospel draws on Jewish and Samaritan traditions of Moses as prophet and king, and Dale Allison (The New Moses, 1993) showed how thoroughly Matthew presents Jesus in Mosaic patterns: rescued from a king who killed infants, called out of Egypt, tested in the wilderness, and teaching from a mountain.

The fit is more than verbal. The people at Horeb asked for a mediator because they could not bear God's voice directly, and God approved. Christians confess that in Jesus God has given the mediator who speaks God's words because he is himself the Word (John 1:1, 14, 18), who says that he speaks just as the Father commanded him (John 12:49-50, echoing verse 18). Hebrews draws the contrast: Moses was faithful as a servant in God's house, but Christ as a son over it (Hebrews 3:5-6), and God, who spoke through the prophets, has now spoken by his Son (Hebrews 1:1-2). Scholars debate whether the passage first promised a single figure or a succession of prophets; many see both, with the line of prophets pointing forward to one who would complete it. The warning of verse 19 also carries over: Hebrews 12:25 urges readers not to refuse the one who speaks.
interpretation:
Jewish interpretation has mostly read the promise as an office. Rashi explained ‘like me’ as meaning that God would raise up prophets from generation to generation, as he raised up Moses. Abraham ibn Ezra (twelfth century) identified the prophet as Joshua, and took ‘like me’ to mean a true prophet of the LORD rather than a diviner. Maimonides built his account of prophecy on this chapter (Mishneh Torah, Foundations of the Torah, chapters 7 to 10): a prophet must be tested repeatedly, a prophecy of good must come to pass, but a prophecy of calamity may be revoked if people repent, as at Nineveh (10:4). His seventh principle of faith holds that Moses' prophecy surpassed that of every prophet before and after him, which shapes Jewish resistance to any claim that a later figure is Moses' equal. The Mishnah defines the false prophet as one who prophesies what he did not hear and assigns his case to a court (m. Sanhedrin 11:1, 5), and it applies the priestly gifts of verse 3 to all ordinary slaughter (m. Chullin 10:1). The synagogue reads the chapter in the portion Shoftim (Deuteronomy 16:18 to 21:9), and the modern rabbi Jonathan Sacks, in his Covenant and Conversation series, used Jeremiah's confrontation with Hananiah to discuss how the test works.

Christians have read the chapter christologically from the start, following Acts 3 and 7. Eusebius of Caesarea (Proof of the Gospel, book 3) argued at length that no later prophet was like Moses as lawgiver and founder of a people and that Jesus alone fits, and in his Church History (1.3) he connected Christ with Israel's anointed prophets, priests, and kings. Jerome's Letter 52 (394) applied the Levites' portion to the clergy. Calvin developed the threefold office of Christ, prophet, priest, and king, in the final edition of his Institutes (2.15, 1559). In the witchcraft controversies of early modern Europe, verses 10 and 11 were among the most cited texts; Reginald Scot's The Discoverie of Witchcraft (1584) expounded the Hebrew terms of this passage at length as part of his case against the witch trials of his day.

Muslim writers from the ninth century, among them Ali ibn Rabban al-Tabari in The Book of Religion and Empire, applied verse 18 to Muhammad, reading ‘their brothers’ as the descendants of Ishmael and pointing to the Qur'an's statement that the unlettered prophet is found written in the Torah (Qur'an 7:157); the argument was popularized in the twentieth century by the South African debater Ahmed Deedat. Modern critical scholarship reads the passage as part of Deuteronomy's law of offices and often as reflecting the prophetic movement of the monarchy; William Holladay argued that Jeremiah saw himself as the prophet like Moses. In the Revised Common Lectionary verses 15 to 20 are read on the Fourth Sunday after the Epiphany in Year B with Mark 1:21-28, where the crowd marvels that Jesus teaches with authority.
text:
English Bibles differ most in the list of verses 10 and 11, because several Hebrew terms are rare and their exact sense uncertain. The King James Version has ‘an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch, or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer’; modern versions use diviner, soothsayer, sorcerer, medium, spiritist, and one who inquires of the dead, and they do not agree on which English word matches which Hebrew term. In verse 10 the Hebrew says literally ‘makes his son or daughter pass through the fire’ (KJV); the BSB and others render “sacrifices his son or daughter in the fire”, a translation that reflects one side of the scholarly debate described in the historical note. In verse 8 the final phrase, literally ‘besides his sales upon the fathers’, is obscure, and translations guess at money from family property or ancestral arrangements.

The ancient versions add their own readings. The Septuagint renders the medium (ov) as engastrimythos, a ventriloquist, and translates blameless in verse 13 with teleios. The Samaritan Pentateuch inserts verses 18 to 22 into the Sinai account of Exodus 20, just after the Ten Commandments, so that the promise is spoken at the mountain itself; the Testimonia from Qumran (4Q175) joins 5:28-29 to 18:18-19 in the same way, showing that this combined form of the text was known in the first century BC. In verse 15, ‘prophet’ is singular in every witness; whether it is a collective singular or refers to one figure is a matter of interpretation, not text. Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same in this chapter.

teach.big: God refuses to be managed by technique and instead gives his people a prophet who speaks his words, a promise that points to Jesus, the prophet like Moses to whom we must listen.

outline.t: Those who serve God at the altar live from the gifts of God's people, and the LORD himself is their inheritance, a picture of what God is to every believer.
In God's household the newcomer shares equally with the established; no one who comes to serve with a willing heart is shut out.
Divination, magic, and consulting the dead are ways of seizing control of the future, and God calls his people to undivided trust instead.
God answers the human need for a mediator by raising up a prophet who speaks his words, and those who hear are accountable to listen.
God's people must test those who claim to speak for him, and they need not fear a word God has not spoken.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first reads verses 1 to 8 as a proof text for tithing or clergy salaries without noticing the Levites' landlessness, which is the point: those who serve God are to depend on him, not accumulate estates. The second treats verses 10 and 11 as a checklist for spotting modern occult activity, or as a license for suspicion and accusation. Christian history shows how badly that can go; the witch trials of early modern Europe cited these verses. The text's concern is where a person seeks security and guidance, which includes respectable modern ways of trying to control the future as well as the exotic ones.

With verses 15 to 19, avoid two opposite errors. One reads the promise so exclusively of Jesus that the succession of Israel's prophets disappears; the other reduces it to the office of prophet and ignores the New Testament's clear claim. With verses 20 to 22, do not turn the test into a formula for dismissing any preacher who is sometimes wrong, and do not present it as the only test. Deuteronomy 13 adds loyalty to the LORD as the deeper test, and Jeremiah 18:7-10 shows that many warnings are conditional. Finally, avoid using verse 20 to justify violence against religious opponents; it belongs to Israel's covenant law under a court, not to the church, whose weapons Paul says are not those of the flesh (2 Corinthians 10:3-5).
teach.pastoral: This chapter will press on people who have been involved in spiritualism, fortune-telling, or occult practice, and on those who, in grief, have sought contact with a dead parent, child, or spouse. The chapter's severity is real, but the reason behind it is the gift of a God who speaks; teach it as an invitation to trust rather than as a sentence of condemnation, and make clear that forgiveness is open. Grief that longs to hear a loved one's voice is human and should be treated with tenderness. The chapter also presses on people who have been harmed by leaders who claimed to speak for God and used that claim to control them. Verse 22 ends with a word for them: do not be afraid of him.

hard.q: Who is the prophet like Moses: a line of prophets, Joshua, Jesus, or someone else?
hard.a:
The strongest objection to the Christian reading comes from Jewish interpreters and from the text's setting. The promise sits among laws about continuing offices (judges, king, priests), so it most naturally describes a continuing office: prophets raised up in each generation. Rashi read it that way, Ibn Ezra identified the first such prophet as Joshua, and many modern critical commentators take ‘prophet’ as a collective singular. Maimonides' seventh principle holds that no prophet ever equals Moses, which rules out any later figure as his true equal, and Jewish readers have long objected that Christians turned an institution into a prediction. A different objection comes from Muslim writers such as Ali ibn Rabban al-Tabari in the ninth century and Ahmed Deedat in the twentieth, who argue that ‘from among their brothers’ points outside Israel to the Ishmaelites and so to Muhammad.

Christian interpreters answer from the text and its history. Deuteronomy's own ending says that no prophet like Moses had arisen (34:10), which shows that the book itself did not think the promise exhausted by Joshua or the prophets who followed. The expectation of a single coming prophet is attested before Christianity, in 1 Maccabees 14:41, the Qumran Community Rule (1QS 9:11), the Testimonia (4Q175), and the Samaritan hope of the Taheb, so the singular reading was not invented by the church. Eusebius argued that only Jesus was like Moses as a mediator of covenant and founder of a people, and Dale Allison has shown how deliberately the Gospels draw the comparison. Against the Islamic reading, Jewish and Christian interpreters note that ‘your brothers’ in Deuteronomy means fellow Israelites: the king must be ‘from among your brothers’ and not a foreigner (17:15), and the Levites have no inheritance ‘among their brothers’ (18:2). Many Christian scholars hold both readings together: the promise established the office of prophet and also pointed beyond it to the one in whom it would be fulfilled. Christians confess Jesus as that prophet; Jewish and Muslim readers disagree, and the disagreement should be stated as honestly as the Christian claim.

hard.q: Is fulfillment really the test of a true prophet, when some biblical prophecies did not come to pass as spoken?
hard.a:
The objection is pressed by skeptical readers and has biblical examples. Jonah announced that Nineveh would be overturned in forty days, and it was not (Jonah 3:4-10). Ezekiel prophesied that Nebuchadnezzar would destroy Tyre (Ezekiel 26:7-14), yet Ezekiel 29:17-20 itself admits that Nebuchadnezzar's army labored against Tyre without reward and promises him Egypt instead; Josephus, citing Phoenician records, says the siege lasted thirteen years (Against Apion 1.156), and the island city fell only to Alexander in 332 BC. Albert Schweitzer (The Quest of the Historical Jesus, 1906) argued that Jesus himself expected the end of the age within his generation and was mistaken. By the standard of verse 22, the objection runs, these prophets would fail.

Several responses have been given. The first is that the Bible states the condition openly: “But if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring” (Jeremiah 18:8). Maimonides drew the same distinction (Foundations of the Torah 10:4), holding that a prophecy of calamity may be revoked through repentance while a prophecy of good must come true, and Richard Pratt (Historical Contingencies and Biblical Predictions, 1993) argued that most predictions carried implicit conditions their hearers understood. The second is that verse 22 is a negative test for plain claims made in the LORD's name, not a rule for reading every warning as a forecast; Micaiah applies it that way to a specific prediction (1 Kings 22:28). The third concerns particular cases: some read Ezekiel 26 as beginning with Nebuchadnezzar and continuing with the many nations of 26:3, and many interpreters, N. T. Wright (Jesus and the Victory of God, 1996) among them, read Jesus' sayings about the end of that generation as fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70. Finally, Deuteronomy 13 makes fulfillment necessary but not sufficient: a prophet whose sign comes true must still be rejected if he leads Israel after other gods. Read together, the two chapters make faithfulness to the LORD the deeper test. How to weigh the particular cases remains debated among faithful readers, and teachers should present the objection fairly.

observe: What do verses 1 to 5 say the Levites receive instead of land, and what does verse 2 say is their inheritance?
List the practices forbidden in verses 10 and 11. What reason does verse 12 give for forbidding them?
According to verses 16 and 17, what had the people asked for at Horeb, and how did God respond?
interpret: Why do you think child sacrifice and fortune-telling appear in the same list? What do they have in common?
What does it mean that the prophet will be ‘like Moses’? What features of Moses would a prophet like him need to share?
How do the test of verse 22 and the test of Deuteronomy 13:1-5 work together? Why would one test alone be insufficient?
apply: Where are you tempted to seek control over an uncertain future rather than trusting God who speaks?
What would it mean for you to say that the LORD is your inheritance, especially in an area where you feel you lack what others have?
How do you weigh the voices that claim to speak for God, and what in this chapter could help you do it more wisely and with less fear?
